response:
Of course!  It’s pretty complex, but I can explain the core elements.  A GPS receiver sends out signals very quickly.  These signals are called “references,” and they’re sent out pretty constantly.  GPS receivers use these references to determine their own position, and the position of other GPS receivers in the vicinity.  In order to calculate any of this, the GPS receiver has to know where it is.  This can be done very accurately, using only the position of the sun, the stars, and the moon.  This location is called “ephemeris coordinates.”

But for most GPS applications, we want to know the location of a GPS receiver in addition to its position.  We call this additional location “geocentric coordinates.”

To determine the geocentric coordinates of a GPS receiver, we must know its position in the sphere-of-influence of the GPS network.  The sphere-of-influence is the area of space surrounding the GPS network, and the exact size of this sphere depends on the type of GPS receiver.  If a GPS receiver is inside a GPS network cell, then its geocentric coordinates are just the position of its receiver in the sphere-of-influence.  If a GPS receiver is outside a GPS network cell, then we must know its position in the sky.  This can be done using a technique called “Differential GPS”, which calculates the difference between the geocentric and ephemeris coordinates, and then uses these to determine the “azimuth” of the GPS receiver.  This last value tells us how far the GPS receiver is from the center of the sphere-of-influence.  The azimuth also tells us the position of the GPS receiver with respect to the GPS network center.  If a GPS receiver is outside, but within a GPS network cell, then the only way to find its geocentric coordinates is by using the azimuth of the cell.  In this case we can use the ephemeris coordinates to calculate the “inclination” of the GPS receiver.  The inclination tells us the angle that the GPS receiver is facing with respect to the GPS network center.  Now we can combine the geocentric coordinates with the ephemeris coordinates to get the position, velocity, and speed of the GPS receiver.
